title: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 1)
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening a three-part series, Linsin argues that teachers struggle year after year with the same difficult students because their compassion overrides doing what's genuinely best for the student. He describes the familiar cycle of managing a difficult student's disruption throughout the year without meaningful change, and identifies compassion-driven excuse-making—rationalizing behavior because of a hard home life or other circumstances—as the root cause that prevents real accountability. Using a hypothetical student named Anthony, Linsin challenges teachers to confront whether they are willing to stop making excuses and hold students to the standard required for success in school. He insists that acknowledging a student's difficult circumstances doesn't require excusing misbehavior, and that believing a student can't overcome their circumstances is itself a way of giving up on them. The article ends with a direct challenge to readers, previewing a strategy in the next installment for how to actually turn such students around.
points: Teachers often struggle with the same difficult students repeatedly because compassion overrides doing what's genuinely best for the student.
Making excuses for misbehavior based on a student's difficult home life or circumstances ultimately harms rather than helps the student.
Understanding the roots of a student's behavior is valid, but it should not translate into excusing or lowering behavioral standards.
Believing a difficult student can't overcome their circumstances is itself a way of giving up on that student.
Real change requires teachers to accept that the power to turn a difficult student around resides with them, not solely with the student's circumstances.
quotes: The reason teachers struggle with difficult students year after year is because they don’t have the stomach for it. Their sense of compassion overrides doing what is right for the student.
But this same compassion that in many respects makes you a good teacher can cause you to make excuses for students, which, in the long run, hurt them and undermine your ability to turn them around.
Are you ready to say, “It’s over. The buck stops here. The disrespect, the bad behavior, and the excuses are going to stop with me?

You really can make a difference in Anthony’s life. You really can change the course of his life and lead him down the path that leads to success and opportunity—despite the terrible hand Anthony has been dealt.
And by excusing bad behavior and blaming it on outside influences, you’re letting them know loud and clear that you don’t believe in them.
